anticolonial.label: Anti-colonial histories
anticolonial.description: Recasts empire through slavery, resistance, liberation, and colonized peoples’ historical agency. Caribbean, African, and other projects develop through different political struggles and intellectual traditions; historical scholarship and theories of decolonization overlap without forming one school.
anticolonial.representative_figures_and_works: C. L. R. James, The Black Jacobins (1938); Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Frantz Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth (1961); Walter Rodney, How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972). Individual entries distinguish their contributions.

representative_people.context: Recasts revolutionary history through enslaved people’s action; successive versions reflect changing political and dramatic concerns.
Makes distinct, disputed arguments about slavery, capitalist development and abolition.
Psychiatrist and political theorist of domination and liberation; not the same kind of historical inquiry as Williams or James.
Connects African economic history, unequal power and popular political education; underdevelopment is a historical relationship.
representative_people.works: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); The Groundings with My Brothers (1969)

representative_people.context: Challenges imperial claims to civilization and examines colonialism’s effects on the colonizer.
Relates culture and liberation to production, class differences and political organization.
representative_people.works: “National Liberation and Culture” (1970), in Return to the Source (1973)

anticolonial.scope_note: James, Williams, Fanon, and Rodney make different arguments. Colonial subjects and liberation politics do not establish one school or Marxist identity. Césaire’s polemic and Cabral’s political theory add distinct questions; cultural struggle and economic explanation can interact. The present Caribbean/African selection does not exhaust anti-colonial historical writing in Asia or elsewhere. Naoroji adds one Indian precursor through a specific1901argument; his use of Mill distinguishes theoretical borrowing from acceptance of colonial policy.

strands.title: Enslaved revolutionaries and historical drama
strands.focus: Popular action and leadership are problems within a changing account of revolution.

strands.title: Slavery, capitalism and abolition
strands.focus: The financing of economic change and explanations of abolition are related but separable disputed claims.

strands.title: Colonial domination and liberation
strands.focus: Political theory and psychiatry supply questions different from an economic history of slavery.

strands.title: Underdevelopment and unequal power
strands.focus: Economic change is placed within relations of colonial control and loss of autonomous decisions.

strands.title: Critique of colonial civilization
strands.focus: Imperial violence challenges Europe’s claims about its own moral progress.

strands.title: Culture, class and liberation
strands.focus: Culture develops through historical social relations and differs within a people; it is not a timeless national essence.

strands.title: Indian drain analysis and borrowed categories
strands.focus: Naoroji applies Mill’s capital propositions to the loss of India’s resources. This earlier Indian case broadens the selection without standing for all Asian anti-colonial thought.

cheikh_anta_diop.label: Cheikh Anta Diop
cheikh_anta_diop.date_label: Nations nègres et culture (1954) · Les fondements économiques et culturels d’un futur État fédéral en Afrique noire (1960) · Antériorité des civilisations nègres (1967) · Civilisation ou barbarie (1981)
cheikh_anta_diop.description: A Senegalese historian whose restoration of African historical consciousness connected Egypt, cultural continuity and Pan-African political projects. Tine distinguishes his programme from Senghor’s négritude and reports Dieng’s objections to its treatment of nationhood and cultural borrowing. Diop’s propositions about Egypt and cultural diffusion remain attributed and contested; neither a common African essence nor agreement among African historians is asserted.
cheikh_anta_diop.representative_figures_and_works: Nations nègres et culture (1954); Les fondements économiques et culturels d’un futur État fédéral en Afrique noire (1960); Antériorité des civilisations nègres (1967); Civilisation ou barbarie (1981).
cheikh_anta_diop.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: Tine’s introduction, section 2 and conclusion in an author-authorized repository; the publisher’s search-rendered account; BnF/INHA metadata; UCAD’s centenary programme metadata. Diop’s books and Dieng’s original critiques are unread. Claims from 1981 and 1989 are mediated through Tine. No verdict on the population of ancient Egypt is established by publisher praise or a commemorative programme. Tine’s death-year error is excluded; UCAD gives 1986. Original French titles and later translations are not conflated.
